content: Insomnia is a sleep disorder characterized by difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or achieving restorative sleep despite having adequate opportunity to sleep. Patients with insomnia often report an inability to quiet their minds or relax enough to fall asleep for more than a few minutes at a time. This condition can result in waking up feeling unrefreshed and experiencing daytime impairment. The first Sleep Disorders Clinic was established at Stanford University in 1970, introducing nocturnal polysomnography and multiple sleep latency tests as diagnostic tools. That same year, benzodiazepines, such as flurazepam, were first promoted for the treatment of insomnia. In 1975, Dr. Dement founded the Association of Sleep Disorders Centers (ASDC), which later declared the Clinical Sleep Society (CSS) in 1984. By 1999, the ASDC was renamed the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. In the 1990s, non-benzodiazepine hypnotics like zolpidem, zaleplon, and eszopiclone became available for insomnia treatment. The FDA approved orexin receptor antagonists, such as suvorexant, in 2005. In 2017, mutations in the CRY1 gene were linked to delayed sleep phase disorder, a condition related to insomnia. The pathophysiology of insomnia is thought to involve several mechanisms, including molecular dysfunction, hyperarousal, the sleep switch model, cognitive and behavioral factors (3P model), and genetic predispositions. Genes implicated in insomnia include APOE4, PER3, 5HTTLPR SNP, CLOCK, HLA-DQB10602, and CRY1. Insomnia can be classified based on its duration into short-term insomnia (lasting less than three months), chronic insomnia (lasting three months or more), and other insomnia disorders. It can also be secondary to other conditions, such as circadian rhythm sleep disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, movement disorders, narcolepsy, or stress. Certain medical conditions, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease, fibromyalgia, epilepsy, migraines, and other headaches, have a bidirectional relationship with insomnia. Routine screening for insomnia is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. However, physicians should inquire about sleep difficulties during patient evaluations. If a patient reports severe or frequent sleep problems, further assessment for insomnia may be warranted. Insomnia must be differentiated from other conditions that cause sleep difficulties, such as normal sleep variants (e.g., short sleepers or excessive time in bed), circadian rhythm disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, movement disorders, narcolepsy, and substanceor medication-induced sleep disturbances. The prevalence of insomnia in primary care settings is estimated to be 10–20%. There is no significant association between insomnia and increased mortality risk. Insomnia is more common in individuals under 35 years of age and does not show a racial predilection, although sleep disturbances are more frequently reported in Black individuals. Risk factors for insomnia include advancing age, poor health, lack of social connections, and female gender. Common complications of insomnia include anxiety, major depressive disorder, and substance abuse. Chronic insomnia is associated with a poor prognosis and may lead to depression, hypertension, and increased mortality in older adults. The diagnostic study of choice for insomnia is a detailed sleep history. Polysomnography is indicated when there is suspicion of an underlying sleep disorder, unusual nocturnal activity, or unexplained severe sleep difficulties. Multiple sleep latency tests are used to evaluate suspected narcolepsy. Actigraphy is helpful in cases of suspected circadian rhythm sleep disorders or when patients cannot provide a reliable sleep history. It is also used for treatment-resistant insomnia. The hallmark symptom of insomnia is difficulty sleeping. A thorough history is essential for diagnosis, including evaluation of potential underlying or coexisting psychiatric or medical disorders. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for insomnia disorder require symptoms to occur at least three times per week for at least three months, cause functional impairment or distress, and not be attributable to another sleep disorder, substance use, or medical/psychiatric condition. Physical examination findings in insomnia are typically normal, although signs of underlying or coexisting medical conditions may be present. There are no specific laboratory, ECG, X-ray, CT, MRI, or other imaging findings associated with insomnia. However, these tests may be useful in diagnosing conditions that contribute to insomnia, such as heart disease or cerebrovascular accidents. Polysomnography may reveal findings of underlying sleep disorders, such as obstructive sleep apnea or periodic limb movement disorder. Multiple sleep latency tests can demonstrate reduced sleep latency and sleep-onset REM periods in narcolepsy. Actigraphy can show increased sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, and nighttime awakenings, as well as decreased sleep efficiency. Pharmacologic treatments for insomnia include benzodiazepines, non-benzodiazepine hypnotics, orexin receptor antagonists, and antihistamines. Surgical intervention is not recommended for insomnia management. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of insomnia.
